items.title: Bangladesh weighs tougher cyber law as AI-generated abuse targets women

s: State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history in the country
Bangladesh is revising its cyber law to tackle AI-generated images, and the draft has triggered a furious debate over how much the state should police speech online.
The ICT Division published the draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act for public comment in mid-September.
It is now with a five-member cabinet committee led by Posts, Telecommunications and ICT Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam.
In a discussion reported on October 19, media figures, legal analysts, and civil society representatives called for the most contested clauses to be removed.
The push follows a campaign season crowded with synthetic media.
Global Voices previously reported on a study that identified 72 AI-manipulated items that gained traction between December 2025 and the February 12, 2026 election.
Synthetic images of political figures were the most common tactic, alongside doctored news-channel graphics.
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which went on to win, was the most frequent target, with 47 cases.
State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history.
Section 57 of the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Act of 2006 punished online content seen as defamatory, hurtful to religious sentiment, or damaging to the state’s image.
A 2013 amendment toughened it, with sentences of up to 14 years.
Journalists and ordinary social media users were among those charged under it.
After years of protest, the government promised to scrap Section 57.
Yet when the Digital Security Act (DSA) was signed into law in October 2018, the same offenses reappeared in sections 25, 28, 29 and 31.
By 2023, the law minister had told parliament that 7,001 cases had been filed under it.
The writer Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody in 2021 after ten months in jail under the DSA, which led to protests at home and abroad.
The Awami League government replaced the DSA with the Cyber Security Act in 2023, but Amnesty International said it repackaged almost all of the DSA’s repressive features.
After the July 2024 uprising, the interim government scrapped nine sections through a new Cyber Security Ordinance in 2025.
Rights groups say hundreds of cases from earlier years are still pending.
Women in politics faced a particular kind of attack.

A Daily Star analysis of AI content before the vote found that pro-Awami League pages targeted female leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) with fabricated images that hinted at moral and sexual impropriety.
After the election, a Prothom Alo fact-check found AI-generated images and invented statements aimed at nominees for reserved women's seats.
Tanvir Mahatab Abir of Rumor Scanner told the paper that visible women, especially in politics, are frequent targets of disinformation.
Not all of it is political.

Data from the Daily Star shows that Facebook pages used deepfake videos of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his family, including his daughter Zaima Rahman, to promote fake “Family Card” offers in exchange for likes and follows.
Among 52 posts analyzed, 13 featured Zaima.
One page administrator told the fact-checking outlet Dismislab that the aim was to gain followers quickly and sell the pages.
In such cases, for many creators of synthetic content, monetization metrics on social platforms often serve as a primary driver alongside political motives.
For ordinary women, the damage can last much longer.
Farzana Sithi, a student activist known for her role in the historic student-led uprising in 2024, was targeted by a fake Facebook profile that Dismislab investigated in March 2025.
Of 166 videos and reels posted between December 13, 2024, and March 17, 2025, 133 were AI-generated deepfakes.
They placed her face on videos of two Indian content creators.
The five most-viewed clips drew more than 4.1 million views, and the account was monetized through Facebook's Stars feature.

items.title: Support Global Voices’ Spotlight: Justice as infrastructure

s: Donate to our Justice as infrastructure Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
All images via Canva or fair use.
Screenshots of Peacekeeping circle (bottom left) and Duterte protest (top center) via YouTube.
International Criminal Court building (top right) via Wikimedia CC BY-SA 4.0.
St. Louis courthouse under construction (center middle) via Picryl CC0 1.0.

Often portrayed as abstract, large, formal, distant, and quite technical, justice is a moral and ethical area, tied to institutions and legal statutes, and can seem a long way from mundane daily experience.
But it is also a deeply practical underpinning for how most societies function.

Without justice systems that work and are understood at the most fundamental level, economic mobility is threatened, socially marginalized groups have no recourse, and lack of trust hampers institutions and interpersonal interactions alike.
Justice is the grease in the motor of social functioning.

Nobody will contest the importance of justice to holding people to a collective moral code of conduct, but the often overlooked next-level function justice plays is that, when justice is fair, fast, and reliable, it makes everything in a society run better.
It allows for a society to fulfill its economic, social, and creative potential.
Copyright law protects ideas and innovation; land law protects resources and livelihoods; labor law supports humane and effective use of our work — as long as those laws are enforced.
When you know that it will be straightforward and predictable to get all the permits, you are more likely to start a business.
When you know that fraud will be punished, you are more likely to invest your capital.
When you know that you will be caught, you’re less likely to evade taxes.
When you know that there will be fair and fast prosecution, you are more likely to report injustice and less likely to perpetrate it.

In this spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to make visible the ways in which justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society, and how countries with a justice deficit can work towards stronger protections that will enable economic and social benefits.

items.title: Warning Signals: Venezuela and the Risk of AI-Powered Chinese Digital Authoritarianism

s: Venezuela could become an early adopter of China’s AI-powered mass surveillance systems.
Former president of Venezuela Nicolás Maduro with current Interim President Delcy Rodríguez and Chinese ambassador in Venezuela Lan Hu.
Photo by Probox.
Used with permission.

Venezuela may be one step away from becoming one of the first countries outside the People’s Republic of China to adopt the new generation of Chinese artificial intelligence systems for mass surveillance and political control, according to a report from the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI).

The report reveals that in July 2025, the Venezuelan government signed a memorandum of understanding with iFlytek, a Chinese company that has been on the U.S. trade sanctions list since 2019 for its role in the repression of Muslim minorities in Xinjiang.
The agreement to jointly develop Artificial intelligence in Venezuela was negotiated by Delcy Rodríguez, then vice president and now Venezuela’s interim president.

The report was written by Fergus Ryan, Bethany Allen, and Nathan Attrill of ASPI’s Cybersecurity, Technology, and Security Program, along with external contributors Mariví Marín (executive director of ProBox ), Shannon van Sant, and analyst Alex Colville.
The report was published in September 2026 by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, with funding from the Human Rights Foundation.

The report, titled “Warning Signals: Venezuela and the Risk of Chinese AI-Enabled Digital Authoritarianism”, documents that Venezuela doesn’t need to build a surveillance system from scratch — it already has one, built largely on Chinese technology through importing cameras, networks, identity systems and command centres from Chinese firms in the past two decades.

While the resulting architecture is fragmented, unevenly deployed and technically constrained, ASPI's researchers identified six interconnected technological layers in the imported surveillance system: telecommunications, digital identity, central databases, video surveillance, internet control, and now, analytics and artificial intelligence.
All of them were built or enhanced with support from companies such as Huawei, ZTE, CEIEC, Hikvision, and Dahua.
At the core of this system’s identity layer is the Carnet de la Patria (Homeland Card), a digital ID linked to social benefits.
The report states it had 21.8 million registered users as of January 2023—roughly three-quarters of Venezuela’s population—and served as many as 14.2 million people each month.
A layer of central databases could cross-reference identity information, biometric data, and social welfare data.

The report also describes a network of video surveillance and command centres (such as the VEN911 and SIMA systems) capable of monitoring public spaces and coordinating responses in real time, and a telecommunications infrastructure that, by channelling a large portion of the country’s data traffic, functions as an additional checkpoint.

While the above technologies were imported through separate contracts, they reinforce one another and form a partially connected surveillance system, enabl ing government agencies to identify, monitor, and take action regarding citizens’ behaviour.

According to the repo rt, iFlytek's AI technology will further integrate the pre-existing layers of surveillance infrastructure into a more comprehensive system, maki ng it faster, more scalable, and harder to evade.

Facial recognition, voice identification, and automated database cross-referencing tools could be used to identify, locate, and profile individuals without any visible human action, such as attending a protest.
iFlytek is one of the world’s leading providers of voice recognition and content moderation technology.

The same report explains that the company promotes a product capable of detecting “more than 100 types” of politically sensitive content in voice messages, and that its technology is integrated into China’s judicial and censorship system.

iFlytek itself already sells a voiceprint identification service that compares recordings against a database to identify a person among thousands; this is precisely the same technology the company has provided to public security authorities in Xinjiang, according to ASPI's report.

items.title: Fish scarcity, tar balls, and stranded dolphins: The hidden costs of offshore platforms in Cameroon waters

s: Oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities
Offshore platform from Garand-Batanga Beach, Kribi South region of Cameroon.
Photo by Leocadia Bongben.
Used with permission.
This story by Leocadia Bongben was produced with the support of Internews’ Earth Journalism Network.
Dede Sluk, 35, a father of three, sits pensively in front of his plank house, fishing nets hanging at the corner, wondering how to fish for his family and prepare his children for school.
Sluk lives in the village of Grand-Batanga 2 in Kribi, in southern Cameroon.
Like many fishermen there, Sluk is annoyed by the lack of access to fish beyond the offshore platforms. He states,
We don’t have access to areas with high fish stock; the Battaillon D’intervention Rapid (BIR), a special army unit guarding the petroleum platform, prohibits passage.
According to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative’s (EITI) 2023 report, oil and gas contributed FCFA 774.51 billion (USD 1.3 million) to Cameroon’s budget.
However, these oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities.

Offshore oil and gas platforms are massive marine structures used to explore, drill, extract, and process petroleum and natural gas from rocky layers beneath the ocean floor; some require the laying of pipes.
The yellow flames and smoke from the Ebome Marine Terminal, a petroleum rig operated by Perenco and SNH west of Grand Batanga, are visible 6.5 kilometers (4.04 miles) from the Kribi coastline.
Two other platforms are the Sanaga 2 offshore facility around Kribi, connected via undersea pipelines from onshore in Bipaga.
West of the Kribi Port is the Kome-Kribi 1 Terminal (FSO), built in 2003, operated by Cameroon Oil Transport Company — the Chad-Cameroon pipeline.
Meanwhile, the Hilli Episeyo, operated by Golar LNG, Perenco, and the National Hydrocarbons Corporation (SNH), departed in July 2026, after eight years.

Among the platforms of concern are those operated by Perenco, a Franco-British company and a prominent player in the oil and gas sector, tagged as an opaque multinational by Friends of the Earth for oil spills, wastewater discharges, gas flaring, and old pipelines crossing rivers.
An Info Congo investigation indicted Perenco for flaring and environmental hazards, endangering the coastal ecosystem and the health of local communities.

Tar balls found in a marine protected area, dolphin and whale strandings, and fish scarcity are hidden costs of offshore oil and gas exploitation, which seems to stall Cameroon’s progress towards the 30×30 marine target under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Laure Ndingue, 50, a mother of five who worked as a fish roaster along Grand Batanga beach for over 10 years, knows that, opposite her charcoal braise, an oil and gas platform sits in the ocean.
She recalls,
Growing up, six barfish were sold for FCFA 500 (USD 0.85); the price jumped to FCFA 1,000 (USD 1.70) and now is FCFA 5000 (USD 8.54) per kilogram.
Even frozen fish is now expensive.
Before, we were not suffering; fish stocks have declined.
Petroleum exploitation is done when the platform is planted on a rock, and most times, the rocks are marine ecosystems that breed fish.

Now, the rocks are occupied by offshore installations, contributing to reduced fish stocks, explains Divine Francois Xavier Mbunje, a fisherman, geologist, and president of the 150-fishermen union at the Grand Batanga beach.
He suggests the government can demarcate platforms and areas of high fish concentration.
About a kilometer or two from the beach, there is no fish, and three kilometers deep, we can have around forty kilograms of fish.

Sluk proposes that oil and gas platforms should help the local population with activities like fish farming, loans to make up for the fish scarcity, recommending that the government provide a loan scheme and subsidize the purchase of motorized equipment, as this will help the fishers go further into the ocean.

items.title: Volunteers from Poland remember how Poles opened their homes to Ukrainian refugees in 2022

s: Now, Russian disinformation fuels the memory of violent historic conflicts, and Polish empathy is burning out

Folkowisko during the “Borderland Memory” project, bringing Ukrainian and Polish youth together to preserve shared historical heritage, restore historic cemeteries, and strengthen cross-cultural friendship.
Photo: Folkowisko.
Used with permission.
Marcin Piotrowski remembers the beginning of his work in Ukraine through the Budomierz-Hruszów border crossing in February 2022, days after the launch of Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“We crossed the border on the second day after the full-scale invasion,” he says, “and there were hundreds of people there.
Nobody was helping them.”
People were waiting for days to enter Poland, some in cars and some on foot, as temperatures fell to around minus 15 degrees Celsius.
On the Polish side, food and transport had been organised, but the queues on the Ukrainian side had become a challenge of their own.
Piotrowski and volunteers from his Polish association, Folkowisko, decided to intervene.
“We had experience because our association organises festivals,” he explains.
“We put up tents, brought volunteers, and our medical service from the festival came as well.
Later, we started helping at other border crossings, then in Lviv at the railway station, and we began working with volunteers from different parts of Ukraine.”
What began as emergency assistance developed into a network of projects across the Polish-Ukrainian border.
Folkowisko helped establish a medical clinic and education centre in Nakhachiv, near the Polish border, where Polish and Ukrainian cultural workers have held joint workshops.
The organisation has also supported psychological care, trained Ukrainian psychologists and social workers, and brought Ukrainian families affected by the war to Poland for temporary respite.
But Folkowisko's work is not only about the present.
Piotrowski is also interested in the history of the border region, and in what happens when difficult memories are discussed through contact rather than isolation.
“Before the Second World War, there were more than a thousand Ukrainians in the village where we work,” he says, referring to a locality in what is now eastern Poland.
“Today, there are 43 people and they are all Polish.
People were resettled in 1945 and 1947, during Operation Vistula.
This was a place where Jews, Poles and Ukrainians lived together, and 80 years ago you could not really say where the border was.”
The history separating the two societies is particularly painful.
During World War II, tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed by Ukrainian nationalist formations in the Volhynia region.
Polish nationalist groups retaliated, killing thousands of Ukrainian civilians.
The competing memories of these events have remained politically sensitive, especially in families whose relatives were victims.
After the fall of communism, the history of Volhynia became increasingly prominent in Polish public debate.

In Ukraine, meanwhile, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) acquired an important place in national memory because of its role in the struggle for Ukrainian independence against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union.
Disputes over monuments, commemorations, exhumations and historical figures have repeatedly affected relations between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The subject is also vulnerable to manipulation, according to Łukasz Wojtkowski, an assistant professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, who researches information operations and disinformation.
He argues that historical grievances can be connected to contemporary fears and used to deepen divisions: “Volhynia is a playbook for propaganda and disguised disinformation,” he explains.
“It is basically the only open case between those two nations that can spark the engine of disinformation and hatred.
Russia can put two irons in the fire at the same time: it can increase the hatred between Poland and Ukraine, and it can reinforce the Russian narrative that there is a fascist regime in Kyiv.”

items.title: Vote young yet govern much later: West African youth’s struggle for power

s: In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely
Youth mobilized in Africa.
Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel
In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18.
In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25.
However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office.
Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.
Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them.
They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves.
The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?
Across the region, the voting age is 18.
However, presidential eligibility ages vary widely.
In Gambia, it’s 30; in Senegal, Nigeria, and Côte d’Ivoire, it’s 35; and in Benin, Ghana, and Guinea, it’s 40.
In the legislative assemblies, the bar is even lower.
In Togo, Benin, Senegal, and Nigeria’s House of Representatives, it’s 25, while in Ghana it’s 21.
The situation in Togo requires closer inspection.
On May 6, 2024, the country legally became a parliamentary republic.
Under the 2024 Constitution, the eligibility age for President of the Republic is 50.
Parliament also now elects the president, whose powers are limited.
Authority now rests with the President of the Council of Ministers, who must be at least 40 and is not elected in public presidential elections.
Faure Gnassingbé has held this position since May 3, 2025, the day parliament also elected the country’s oldest-ever incoming president of the Republic, Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, 86.
However, the country’s legal age limit is hardly set in stone.
In 2002, the National Assembly lowered it from 45 to 35 — a reform the opposition called tailor-made for Faure Gnassingbé.

More recently, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, on July 30, 2026, the Ghanaian government agreed in principle to lower the minimum presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35, defying the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendation of 30.
This legislation will ultimately go to a referendum, requiring a 40 percent turnout and a 75 percent approval.
In 2018, Nigeria set a regional precedent.
Under pressure from the youth-led Not Too Young To Run campaign, the law lowered the presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35 and the House of Representatives’ eligibility age from 30 to 25.
According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union, lowering the minimum presidential age leads to younger parliaments.
However, Côte d’Ivoire tells a very different story.
In 2016, after removing the maximum age limit of 75 to run for office, incumbent President Alassane Ouattara, 83, ran for another term in 2025.
The law rarely protects younger generations.
Even though young people have the right to vote across the continent, that does not mean all young people exercise that right.
In August 2025, an Afrobarometer survey found that those aged 18 to 35 were less active than their elders in almost all traditional means of political participation.
Overall across the continent, they trailed by 18 percentage points in voting, but by a record 29 points in Senegal.
Protests were the only exception.
In Togo’s capital of Lomé, the June 6 Movement, sparked by the rapper Aamron’s arrest, brought thousands of people onto the streets.
According to the Media Foundation for West Africa, the subsequent crackdown, for which the International Federation for Human Rights ( FIDH) blamed government-backed militiamen, left seven dead.

items.title: Queer mediums of the cult of María Lionza are redefining the gender binary in Venezuela’s sacred mountain

s: Gender diversity, resistance and ritual cross-dressing in Venezuela's sacred cult
Portrait of Wander Rodríguez, part of the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers, and the LGBTIQ+ community.
Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.
In Venezuela, Spiritism as a religion is part of the collective imagination, of our identity; popular beliefs and ritual practices that take us back to our ancestors in colonial times.

Over the years, Spiritism has evolved into a vibrant, contemporary national cult centered on the figure of María Lionza as the principal protector of waters and the charms of nature, a figure who challenges the notions of the patriarchal state and opposes monotheistic religions.

This religious system has been studied in depth by anthropologists in our country ( Daisy Barreto, Angelina Pollak-Eltz, Michelle Asencio, Francisco Ferrándiz, Cesar Escalona, among others), which I had read about and found interesting at the time, but which I later witnessed for the first time in its most important sites, such as Quibayo and Sorte, in the state of Yaracuy, Venezuela.
Altar to María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.

These sites are part of the Cerro María Lionza Natural Monument, popularly known as the Montaña de Sorte, and they represent the most prominent expressions of this cult nationwide, so they are visited year-round by practitioners or “caravans” (as these groups are commonly called),
But few days are as important as October 11 and 12, when thousands of people flock there to celebrate the Day of Indigenous Resistance in Venezuela.

These dates offer an opportunity for ethnographic and cultural observation, specifically how oral histories and our ethnic origins are reclaimed; including those of Indigenous peoples, some of them warriors who fought against Spanish colonization, and African populations — enslaved people and maroons [AN: this will need context] — as we can understand through the figure of the Three Powers: Queen María Lionza as the central figure of the cult, the leader, accompanied by El Indio Guaicaipuro and El Negro Felipe.
Altar to Queen María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.

For this celebration families gather among the trees and along the banks of the Yaracuy River, which runs through the entire mountain, setting up lavish altars to the various deities of Venezuelan spiritualism, which embody the sacred rituals characteristic of the Marialioncero cult.

The figure of María Lionza is profound, and I believe it is risky to oversimplify her, as she is regarded as a Queen, a Goddess, a mother, and a guardian, yet there are also aspects linked to her sensuality, as evidenced by the iconographic representations of her that have emerged -naked or clothed, for example-.

In this regard, I draw upon the writings of Francisco Ferrándiz and César Escalona from the perspective of Venezuelan anthropology, combining them with my own observations and field interviews, to address issues related to gender and sexual diversity that are essential to the fascinating debate within the cult on its various courts — such as the Black Court, the Viking Court, the Malandra Court, the Chamarrera Court, and the Medical Court, among others — and entities.
Detail of flowers and bottles of the Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.

The Sorte Mountain is a setting where gender stereotypes are called into question, and I believe they undermine androcentric perspectives and rigid notions of masculinity and femininity found within Christianity, since the entities pose a challenge due to their wide spectrum in terms of strength, height, voice, attire, and other details of the mediums who embody them, as well as the particular characteristics of each spirit.
Strenght between banks and Viking Court entity.
Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12.
Freisy González Portales.
Used with permission.

items.title: Between two shores: The ‘Monhés,’ nationality, and a sense of belonging in Mozambique

s: Being Mozambican is a matter of belonging — regardless of one’s origin, appearance, or surname
Indians in Mozambique celebrating the Hindu festival of Navratri.
Image by Kash_if via Flickr. CC BY 2.0.
In Mozambique, the word monhé has a much deeper history than its everyday use might suggest.
Depending on who says it and the context, it can simply be a reference to the population of Indian origin, an identity marker, or a prejudiced remark.
But behind the word there is a history of migration, trade, colonialism, independence, displacement, and, above all, belonging.
The question of who is Mozambican gets particularly interesting when we look at the communities of Indian origin, who have lived in the country for several generations.
Are they Mozambicans? Indians? Foreigners?
Or, in some cases, stateless persons?
The answer cannot be found in appearance, surname, religion, or family origin alone.
It is found in the country’s history and, particularly, in its nationality law.

The presence of people originating from the Indian subcontinent in the lands we now call Mozambique predates the country’s independence and, in many instances, predates the demarcation of the current political borders.
The Indian Ocean’s trade networks connected the East African coast to South Asia long before 1975, the year Mozambique gained its independence.
Over time, merchants, families, and whole communities settled in different parts of the country.
During the Portuguese colonial period, this took place within a political structure that gave people nationalities and legal statuses according to the rules of the empire.
As such, “being of Indian origin” never meant automatically “being an Indian citizen.
A person can have Indian ancestry and at the same time hold Portuguese, Indian, Pakistani, or any other nationality, which could leave people in a complex bureaucratic situation.
This distinction became especially important when the empire came to an end.
Mozambique’s independence, made official on June 25th, 1975, did not just mean a transfer of political power.
It also implied the need to define who would legally receive the new state, which was known as the New State.
The Nationality Law of 1975 was key to answering that question.

Among its provisions were rules that recognized as Mozambicans certain people born in the territory and resident in Mozambique at the time of independence, as well as other criteria related to birth, family links, and residence.
The legislation would thus transform a heterogeneous imperial population into a national political community.

For many families of Indian origin who lived in Mozambique for decades or generations, this transformation would mean a fundamental change: no longer being legally associated with a colonial power or a foreign nationality and becoming part of the new Mozambican nation.
But the experience of this transition was not the same for everybody.
Decolonization created situations where identity, origin, and nationality did not match.
Imagine a family history across three generations: the grandparents born in India, the parents born in Mozambique during the colonial period, and the children born after independence.
Which nationality should each generation have?

The answer may depend on specific legal circumstances: place of birth, the parents’ nationality, residence in Mozambique at its independence, existing documentation, and any decisions to opt for or relinquish nationality.
Here, the issue of statelessness arises.
A stateless person is somebody who is not considered a national by any state’s legislation.
It is not an ambiguous cultural identity or feeling divided between two countries, but a legal status.

After decolonization, some people in former colonial territories, such as Angola and Mozambique, faced this problem: some were no longer recognized as nationals by the former colonial power without any other nationalities automatically being granted.
This does not mean, though, that the whole Indian community in Mozambique became stateless.
This generalization would be historically and legally incorrect.

items.title: Big Tech and authoritarian states: Belarus

s: A Global Voices video podcast on the state of digital repression in Belarus
There are more autocracies in the world in 2026 than there are democracies.
Some researchers identify digital authoritarianism as the use of digital technology by regimes to surveil, repress, and manipulate domestic and foreign populations.
Others argue that the same practices are also carried out by hybrid and democratic regimes.
However, they can not execute them without major tech companies becoming complicit, with or without their knowledge.
Typically, when speaking about digital authoritarianism, academics and media talk about China and Russia (and occasionally Iran and Syria).
However, countries such as Belarus (or Eritrea, Nicaragua, Afghanistan, Myanmar) that consistently rank as more authoritarian than China are rarely discussed.
Global Voices invited an expert on Belarusian internet, digital rights and media, Mikhail Doroshevich, on the GV video podcast “Big Tech and Authoritarian States.

We discussed why Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenka’s regime is not blocking Western social media platforms, how the internet and self-censorship are weaponized, and how platforms help the regime to spread its propaganda.
You can view and listen to the podcast in Russian on our YouTube Channel and read the translated transcript below:
Daria Dergacheva (DD): Hello, dear viewers.
My name is Daria Dergacheva, and welcome to another Global Voices video podcast.
Today we are discussing Big Tech and authoritarian states.
Our guest is Mikhail Doroshevich, who works on digital issues in Belarus.
We will speak in Russian, but an English translation and subtitles will be available.
Please leave your questions in the comments and like the video.
Mikhail, welcome.
Please tell us a little about yourself.
This is the second Global Voices video podcast I have hosted, and today we want to focus on Belarus.
Mikhail Doroshevich (MD): I can describe myself very briefly, in one sentence: I am a researcher who has been studying the Belarusian internet for more than 30 years.
A well-known political scientist once introduced me in a publication as a “veteran of the Belarusian internet.
Since then, I have jokingly used that description myself.
But let us talk about something more interesting.
DD: Being a veteran of the Belarusian internet is interesting in itself!
I would also like to talk about its history and what is happening now.
I recently saw an article from Carnegie suggesting that the internet in Belarus remains considerably more open than in Russia.
I find this paradox fascinating.
How does the Belarusian regime deal with Western, Chinese, and Russian platforms?
MD: That is quite a complicated technical question.
In infrastructural terms, the Belarusian internet has always been more restricted than the Russian internet.
By infrastructure, I mean connectivity and connections to the global internet.
Since the 1990s, Russian internet providers and mobile telecommunications companies have had their own international connections.
Belarus, by contrast, has always had a vulnerable infrastructure.
International connections were controlled by state-owned companies, including the national operator.
Private providers and mobile operators never had their own independent international connections.
Yet today Russia restricts access to many social media services, from LinkedIn onwards, while Belarus does not impose comparable restrictions on those platforms.
So Belarus historically had greater technical constraints, and shutdowns regularly accompanied political campaigns.
Blocking websites and resources designated as extremist or terrorist is still widespread and ongoing.
But Belarus has not followed the path Russia has taken in recent years.
Their technological approaches have diverged.
DD: Do you think the platforms comply with [blocking or takedown] requests from the Belarusian state?
Why is this happening?

items.title: In Brazil’s elections, big techs’ transparency and cooperation policies translate as governance washing, according to this expert

s: Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University NetLab has been following closely how this election unfolds on social media
Amid a series of corruption scandals, the 2026 general election in Brazil is also flooded with headlines about social media companies’ role in the campaign.

Users supporting the candidacy of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the incumbent center-left candidate running for re-election, have been reporting a sudden drop in their Instagram Stories views when posting about politics.

They say that Meta AI refused to generate images featuring Lula’s name and party number, while delivering the same request for Flávio Bolsonaro, his far-right opponent and the son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro.
On October 16, Meta admitted technical problems on its platforms which affected how pro-Lula content was delivered to users.

As reported by the Associated Press, despite acknowledging “global technical glitches, strict anti-fraud measures, and regulatory compliance rather than targeted suppression,” the company that owns Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook denied any political bias.

Lula filed a complaint against Meta accusing the company of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favor Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election, with a judge from the country’s top electoral court ruling that Meta must adopt measures to ensure equal treatment.
With an estimated population of 214 million, Brazil is an important market for social media platforms.
It ranks as the second country by number of WhatsApp users and saw the internet become a key component of Jair Bolsonaro’s ascent around 10 years ago.

To understand the current election scenario, Global Voices spoke to Nicole Sanchotene, project coordinator at NetLab, a research laboratory at Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University (UFRJ) that has been publishing reports on the impact of big tech on the electoral campaign.
The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
Global Voices: What have you identified in NetLab’s recent reports about the elections?
Nicole Sanchotene: É muito difícil avaliar o impacto e os possíveis efeitos para a disputa eleitoral e para a percepção das pessoas.

O problema central que a gente tem apontado é sobre transparência, uma certa normalização de possíveis ilícitos eleitorais, pontos que são consenso na resolução do TSE (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral) e não estamos vendo cumprimento pleno das plataformas.
O Kwai, que é uma plataforma com ampla adesão no Brasil, tem mais de 60 milhões de usuários, é bastante usado pelas classes C e D, fez uma parceria com o TSE e não está adequado.
Não atende a requisitos básicos, a biblioteca de anúncios político-eleitorais tem falhas no tipo de dado que entrega.
A gente tem chamado essas práticas de transparência de fachada.
Cada uma das plataformas tem um problema específico.
Seja por dados incompletos, seja pela veiculação ou recomendação de conteúdo que não deveria ser recomendado.

O que a gente vê é que elas não estão respeitando plenamente o que é exigido pelas normas brasileiras para garantir um mínimo de condições de igualdade para os candidatos, condições que permitam um ambiente de informação, de propaganda, seguro para os usuários e para a disputa eleitoral.
Nicole Sanchotene: It’s hard to evaluate the impact and possible effects on the running and on people’s perception.

The central issue that we’ve been pointing to is transparency, a certain normalization of possible illicit electoral practices, issues that were agreed upon in the TSE [Superior Electoral Court, Brazil's top electoral court] resolution, and we are not seeing the platforms comply fully.

Kwai, a platform with widespread adoption in Brazil, with over 60 million users and largely used by “ C and D classes ” [lower income groups and the basis of the socio-economic pyramid], partnered with the electoral court, and it’s not suitable yet.
It doesn't meet basic requirements; their library for political-electoral ads has flaws in the data delivered.
We have been calling this a ‘façade of transparency.’

items.title: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, children with Down syndrome are using a video game to safely navigate the internet

s: A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game
SafeClick is a video game that teaches children with Down syndrome about digital safety.
A virtual assistant, Sol the Owl, that guides them through the game.
Image by the game's developers, used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web.

This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ concerns about digital safety and the risks of being online.
There are approximately 550-700 children and adolescents with Down syndrome in the country.
They are supported by three specialized associations nationwide: the Association “Life with Down Syndrome of FBiH ”, Down Syndrome Association Mostar, and DOWN SY I MI.

To teach online safety, these organizations have to rely on online safety tools that heavily feature text, abstract explanations, and complex language, which are not accessible or meaningful for children with Down syndrome.
A group of developers, IT professionals, and designers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been working to address the lack of a digital safety tool tailored to children and adolescents with Down syndrome.
Their goal is to help young people understand, practice, and feel confident making decisions online.

Global Voices conducted a written interview over email with Stefan Filipovic, a member of this group, to learn how they created a video game to teach children with the genetic condition about digital safety.
The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.
Stefan Filipovic (SF): We are a group of IT professionals, developers, and designers from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Most of our work is in commercial technology, but we also have experience developing educational and socially useful video games, such as Eureka – Edukativna videoigra, an educational game for children, and Lea & Leo, a game about children with diabetes.
We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to use that experience for a group that, in our opinion, is often overlooked when digital products are designed.
Young people with intellectual disabilities are using phones and the internet, but many digital tools are simply not designed with their needs in mind.
The video game SafeClick ( Siguran klik ) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

SF: While working with Servis Centar “Dajte nam šansu – Zvjezdice” – an association and day center that provides free support to children, young people, and people with developmental disabilities, we saw that young people with Down syndrome were using phones and the internet, but there were very few cyber-safety resources made specifically for them.
Most materials use a lot of text, complicated explanations, or interfaces that are difficult to follow.
To our knowledge, parents and educators often end up focusing on limiting internet use rather than teaching young people how to deal with unsafe situations.

items.title: Complementary forces: Why activism needs art to drive action

s: ‘A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention.’
An urban art piece called “The Post is fast, it's only the letters that arrive slowly” in front of the main Post Office in Skopje, North Macedonia.
In recent decades, practices that bring art directly into people’s everyday lives have become increasingly common.
They may be initiated by artists, activists, informal groups, or citizens who use creative means to draw attention to a problem, express disagreement, or call for change.
Public spaces become a place where an action meets an audience, provokes a response, and starts a conversation.
This approach, when artistic and creative means are used to press for solutions or encourage social change, is called artistic activism.
The “Monument to Diazepam” raised awareness about overuse of prescription drugs.
Photo by Nikola Pisarev.
Used with permission.
At their core, art and activism have different but complementary roles.
Activism seeks to change a situation through strategic planning and advocacy; art, on the other hand, is not pro or against but can move people emotionally.
Art can change how people see and experience a situation.
It opens up new perspectives and associations, and its effects are not always immediate or easy to measure.
Artistic activism brings these possibilities together: It uses the emotional experience of art as a prompt for action and directs that action towards change.
Urban art actions in North Macedonia offer local examples for exploring this approach.
Many actions were developed through direct engagement with specific problems, rather than as part of a broader methodology.
They began with a desire to point out an injustice, raise a question, or help address a problem.
Urban art action “Fishing for Potholes” in Veles, North Macedonia, which included public performance and distribution of photo and video coverage.
Photo by Nikola Pisarev.
Used with permission.
It does not always take a large crowd to draw attention to a problem.
A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention even when it is created by a small group — or by a single person.
This does not replace the power of mass organizing, but it makes action possible when resources are limited.
Additionally, amid the constant barrage of information, an unusual sculpture, a witty message, or an intervention in public space can interrupt people’s routine scrolling.
They may photograph and share the action, extending its reach beyond the place where it took place through social media and communication platforms.
Still, a high number of views does not mean the problem has been solved.
Visibility is an opportunity that needs to be connected to the action’s purpose.
Within high-risk or authoritarian contexts, creative action can also give activists greater room to act, even under pressure.
Humor, metaphor, and unexpected forms can sometimes make a problem visible without direct confrontation.
In some cases, the people behind an action can also remain anonymous.
This does not make them immune to pressure: The level of risk depends on the context, the subject, and the way the action is carried out.
But a creative form may allow organizers to absorb some of that pressure while keeping the affected community less exposed.
Likewise, a problem hidden in reports, procedures, or individual experiences can remain invisible to the larger public.
An artistic action can translate a complex situation into an image, object, or scene that people can readily recognize.
This can encourage citizens, experts and decision-makers to discuss the problem and possible solutions.
The challenge is to make the message clear without distorting the substance of the issue.
Art also has a way of enduring long after it has disappeared from public space.
A scene, symbol, or object can become a story that the media and the public continue to share after the intervention has ended.

items.title: Venezuela faces a deepening energy crisis as protests grow

s: For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life
This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “ Protest in Democracy.
With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy.
You can support this coverage by donating here.
“Yesterday we didn't have electricity for 11 hours.

The day before, it was seven,” explains Yanira, a 33-year-old artist and designer who lives with her ailing 73-year-old father in Maracaibo, one of the cities most affected by Venezuela’s electricity rationing.
In a region where temperatures remain high throughout much of the year, going without electricity is more than an inconvenience.
For her family, the blackouts directly affect their health, work and daily routines.
Across the country, increasingly long and unpredictable blackouts are disrupting work, education, businesses and sleep.
In several cities, frustration has spilled into the streets, with residents protesting outages and blocking roads in the darkness.
In August, residents of various cities, including Turmero and Valencia, took to the streets at night to protest the worsening situation.
Their demonstrations came as authorities expanded electricity rationing in response to growing pressure on the country’s fragile power grid.
The crisis is particularly severe outside Caracas, where scheduled outages lasting between six and 15 hours a day have been reported in several regions.
Authorities have also introduced shorter working hours for some public sector employees, and reached an agreement with shopping malls to reduce electricity consumption.
The government has attributed the worsening shortages in part to the effects of El Niño, which has brought drought and unusually high temperatures to Venezuela.
There is also, however, a series of factors worsening the situation, like the major failure at Guri Hydroelectric plant, where one of its turbines — which generated 770MW — collapsed.
The country’s electricity problems long predate the current weather conditions.

Venezuela’s power system has suffered from years of underinvestment, poor maintenance and allegations of corruption, resulting in a system that is increasingly unable to meet the country’s electricity needs.
For residents of Maracaibo, one of Venezuela’s largest and most economically important cities, the crisis has become deeply personal.
Yanira says she can spend at least six hours a day without electricity.
The outages have affected both her livelihood and her mental health.
She has had a hard time finding a job or even working remotely, because blackouts make it difficult to function.

She eventually began running small businesses from home, first selling sandwiches and cepillados zulianos — shaved-ice treats popular in the region — but keeping food frozen and drinks cold is a constant challenge when electricity can disappear without warning:
The hardest moments come at night.
Without air conditioning, sleeping becomes difficult in Maracaibo’s intense heat — and while opening the windows brings some relief, it also lets tropical insects inside.
Yanira says the situation has affected her sleep so severely that she began taking sleeping pills.
Her experience reflects a broader problem.
According to Venezuela’s 2025 Living Conditions Survey, only around 10 percent of Venezuelans live without experiencing power outages.
For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life.
The blackouts are also taking a toll on local economies.

The National Chamber of Commerce reported that 38 percent of businesses had closed during the year, amid the combined effects of the electricity crisis and the country’s broader economic difficulties.
The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage, and copyright law is no exception
“Oh!
Bob Marley, right?
Jamaican culture has been popularised by the mainstream, and as a Jamaican-American, I often get a glimpse into how others have consumed it and from what point of view.

I would not call myself an ardent Marley fan, but I know the kind of people who are most likely attached to his music outside of Jamaica — for example, the potential counterculture student of the 1970s at UCLA who found connection to his messages of resistance.

My personal fascination with Jamaican music is the “riddim” — the Jamaican patois spelling of “rhythm” — an instrumental beat or tune constructed not for a single artist, but to be used by the collective of the time and to be both enjoyed and critiqued by the culture makers of Jamaican art: the disenfranchised masses.
As a public interest technologist and digital rights advocate, I view the “riddim” with an open-source lens.
It helped to protect Jamaican culture, particularly from Western constructs that are heavily embedded in existing power dynamics like rigid copyright laws and the corporate commodification of music.
Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.
Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party.

In Larisa Kingston Mann’s “ Rude Citizenship,” she outlines how copyright law was written at a time when many of the island’s people were themselves considered property under slavery, thereby creating — from the very start — a contentious relationship with those holding the society’s wealth.
Copyright law was set up for those with ample resources to dictate what could be protected and who could profit.
Beat-sharing directly challenges neo-colonial copyright’s individualistic definition of ownership and originality.
Traditional copyright promotes monopoly over expression, enforced by harsh legal mechanisms (such as statutory damages ) that make intertextuality, reuse, and artistic experimentation legally risky.
Even Sean Paul, one of the most commercially successful dancehall artists in the world, attributed his mainstream success of “Get Busy” to the Diwali Riddim.
If not for this collective creativity and shared use, we would not see dancehall music evolve and get pushed to the world in the way that it has.
Collective sharing didn’t stop at just music; dance was often learned collectively as well.
I used to watch “ passa passa ” videos in high school and college, just to learn and keep up to date with the latest dances coming out of Jamaica and New York City in the early 2000s.
These parties were the bane of anyone entrenched in respectability.
The clothes were outlandish, the manners “rude,” the dancehall queens nothing short of acrobatic, and the parties could go until 6:00 a.m.

But this was also the time when new artists could get a slot, vendors could make a little money, and producers could collaborate with artists and get public consensus on what worked before dropping money at a studio.
The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage in many ways, and copyright law is no exception.
Jamaica was often sidelined into less than favourable international trade agreements that didn’t keep the interests of the Jamaican masses in mind.

More often than not, there was a strict one-size-fits-all structure, dictated by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank: detrimental loan structures, one-sided economic trade agreements, currency devaluation, and exploitative labour guidelines.

items.title: Independent journalism under siege in Georgia

s: Need for a unity became urgent in April 2025, after the law on approval of foreign grants
This article by Elli Kostika is an edited version of a longer piece, first published on June 11, 2026, by the non-profit journalism organization Incubator for Media Education and Development (iMEdD).
This excerpt is published on Global Voices, with permission under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license.
Any use of images or charts by third parties requires permission.

As Georgia has dropped to 135th place in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, iMEdD spoke with representatives of four independent media outlets about the challenges facing journalism in the country: imprisonments, attacks, “foreign agent” laws, and the struggle for survival.
Tamar Rukhadze, Deputy Director of Georgian outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti, describing the state of Georgia’s press, said:

Ι cannot remember any other period in Georgia’s recent history, since I’ve started as a journalist in 1997, with such a harsh and hostile environment towards journalists, media workers and civil society.
Georgia’s government, led by the Georgian Dream party, has intensified its crackdown on media by adopting a series of restrictive laws aimed at suppressing the country’s independent media.
Meanwhile, Georgian journalists have been facing constant threats, from legal challenges to physical attacks.

Georgia’s deteriorating press freedom is part of a broader process of democratic backsliding, with the right to peaceful protest severely restricted, opposition politicians jailed, a decline in judicial independence, and a disputed election in October 2024.
Although Georgia has been an EU candidate country since 2023, the ruling Georgian Dream Party, founded by oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, has pivoted the country’s foreign policy towards Russia.

However, large segments of Georgia’s population remain pro-EU, and citizens have been protesting for over 500 consecutive days since November 2024, following the contested October 2024 elections and the government’s decision to suspend efforts to advance Georgia’s EU accession process until 2028.
As the struggles of Georgia’s independent journalists have intensified in this increasingly repressive environment, so too has their determination to survive.
Batumelebi and Netgazeti have paid a heavy price for their independence.
The outlets’ co-founder and CEO, Mzia Amaglobeli, was arrested on January 12, 2025, after an altercation with a police chief in Batumi, Georgia’s second-largest city.
Following a trial which press freedom groups denounced as politically motivated, Amaglobeli has been sentenced to two years in prison.
In December 2025, the European Parliament awarded her the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought.
She remains detained under deplorable conditions.

Her eyesight — already poor before her imprisonment — is now almost completely lost, Rukhadze tells us, while her lawyers spent six months securing permission for her to visit a clinic, as medical facilities within the penitentiary system lack proper equipment.
In an interview with iMEdD, Rukhadze stresses the deep psychological effects Amaglobeli’s sentence has had on the newsrooms.
“ We aren’t the same as we were earlier before this imprisonment,” adding, “It’s a nightmare for every single journalist to become news.”
Rather than resorting to self-censorship, Batumelebi’s and Netgazeti’s journalists have persisted in their reporting.
She highlights:

The first thing Mzia did after her arrest was to send a message from prison, asking her team to continue their work as before — to do what they had always done and what they are known for: professional, ethical watchdog journalism that gives a voice to those who need it most.
Arrests and detainments are only one of the ways the Georgian government uses legislation against the country’s independent media.

Nino Bakradze, co-founder and editor-in-chief of iFact, tells iMEdD they have lost 90 percent of their income since May 2025 owing to a series of laws that have restricted the outlet’s access to foreign funding.

items.title: What telecoms leave behind when they exit a country

s: When telecoms pull out of markets, data protection and human rights commitments often disappear

In March 2022, just over a year after Myanmar’s military coup, Telenor, the Norwegian telecommunications giant, sold its subsidiary in the country to M1 Group, bringing nearly eight years of operation to an end.
But leaving Myanmar did not end the controversy surrounding its departure.
Instead, the hasty exit came back to haunt the company over the next four years.
Since then, criticisms, lawsuits and litigation by civil society and affected people have continued to follow the company.

The scrutiny also reached a crescendo this September, when Norwegian authorities opened criminal investigations into Telenor over allegations of aiding crimes against humanity in the country and transferring sanctioned surveillance equipment during the sale.
Within days, a court in Norway also green-lit a class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of a group of Telenor’s former customers in Myanmar.
Telenor reiterated its position upon the investigation, arguing that any alternatives would have endangered the employees’ lives.

Yet the company’s trouble raises a broader question that many telecommunication multinationals may have to confront one day: When a company decides to exit a “high-risk market,” where does its responsibility end?
Under military rule, Telenor faced government demands to facilitate surveillance, hand over the personal data of dissidents and activists, and restrict access to information.
In a market like this, staying may cease to be viable.

For a telecom operator, the matter is not simply to make a choice between remaining in the market or leaving, but whether it can exit in a way that minimizes further harm to users, without leaving them more vulnerable.
Unfortunately, Telenor failed to do so.
In a conventional asset sale involving multinational companies, the transaction may center largely around physical and commercial assets, such as factories, equipment, and inventory.
Selling a telecom subsidiary is another story.
As gatekeepers of internet access and digital information, telcos control sensitive user data, including location records and device logs.
They also serve as key intermediaries for interception systems and have the technical capacity to cut off network access.
In a sale, the company hands over not just infrastructure and commercial assets, but also systems and data that can expose the movements and footprints of millions of users.

Without rigorous buyer scrutiny and assessments of the risks associated with the transfer, a corporate sale may lead to grave harm to users, who might be watched, tracked, or even silenced in authoritarian contexts.
What followed in Myanmar showed that the risk was anything but hypothetical.
It also revealed why powerful companies cannot simply shed their responsibilities by selling their business, when people depending on their services are left to bear the consequences.
This matters because Telenor’s withdrawal from Myanmar is hardly an isolated case.
After the debacle, the telecom giant began systematically pulling back from its Asian markets.
In 2022, the company combined its Malaysian subsidiary Digi with local telecom service Celcom.
In Thailand the following year, it merged its local business dtac with True Corporation before later selling down most of its stake in the entity.
It also completed its sale of Telenor Pakistan to PTCL at the end of 2025, with further plans to dispense with its remaining Asian assets.
Zooming out, multinational telecom operators are shrinking the overseas footprints they spent decades building.
MTN, Africa’s largest telecom operator, announced its plan to “ orderly exit ” from the Middle East in 2020 amid geopolitical risks.
The company has ended its operations in Syria, Yemen, and Afghanistan by 2025.
MTN also completed the sale of its operations in Guinea-Bissau and Guinea-Conakry in 2024, citing unsustainable costs.

items.title: Palestine is already living under the Big Tech authoritarianism the world is being sold

s: Emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control
An aerial view showing destruction in Rafah, Gaza Strip, on January 21, 2025.
Photo by Ashraf Amra on Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO ).
For Palestinians, the relationship between technology and authoritarianism is a lived reality, rather than predictions or science fiction.
Israel’s settler-colonial regime has long fused military force with legal, economic and technological mechanisms to dominate Palestinian life.
Surveillance, data harvesting, facial recognition, telecommunications blackouts, digital censorship and algorithmic systems are now woven into this architecture of control.

The genocidal war on Gaza has exposed the consequences with devastating clarity, where technologies built to collect, process and classify information have been absorbed into systems that surveil, target and kill Palestinians.
But Palestine is also a warning about what comes next.
Technologies developed, tested and refined under occupation do not stay there.
They become products, expertise and business models that circulate globally.

What emerges is a political economy in which military and intelligence institutions, technology companies, investors and governments converge around the extraction and processing of data as a means of exercising power.

This is one of the central arguments of Digital Domination, a publication of The Arab Center for the Advancement of Social Media ’s Maryam Abu Daqqa Fellowship, which brings together five studies on artificial intelligence, surveillance, data extraction and corporate power in Palestine and beyond.
The fellowship is named after Maryam Abu Daqqa, a Palestinian journalist murdered by Israel in Gaza in August 2025 while documenting life under siege.
Across different cases, the research points to the same transformation, showing how emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control.
It is becoming their infrastructure.
Israel’s surveillance industry shows this plainly.
It operates through intimate ties between military and intelligence institutions, private companies, venture capital and international markets.
Tools tested on Palestinians are refined, repackaged as commercial products and exported to the world as security solutions.
This is no accident of a thriving tech sector.
It is a political and economic system in which security technologies gain value precisely because of their capacity to monitor, classify and control populations.
The violence these systems enable is increasingly literal.

Investigations into Israel’s AI-assisted targeting systems, including Lavender, The Gospel and Where’s Daddy, have documented how machine-learning systems and mass surveillance data have been folded into the identification and targeting of Palestinians in Gaza.

A new film, NAZA, produced by The Guardian and built on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders, details the secret systems used to select people for bombing in their homes at night, in the knowledge that their families would be killed, too.

At a military conference in London in late June, an executive from the Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems presented a slide crediting its digital command system with 850,000 “real-time intel targets” across Gaza and Lebanon between October 2023 and the end of 2025.
The company has since tried to recast the figure as aggregate system activity, a claim that sits uneasily with the slide itself.
The significance is not that an algorithm has replaced human violence.
It is that these systems increase the scale, speed and bureaucratic distance at which violence is organised, while cloaking life-and-death decisions in the appearance of technical objectivity.

In June, Amnesty International and more than 100 other signatories warned that systems such as Lavender, Gospel and Where’s Daddy dilute human responsibility and obscure international crimes behind a veneer of algorithmic objectivity.
The same architecture extends beyond weapons.

At 7amleh, we have documented how platforms suppress Palestinian speech, how state-linked actors use commercial platforms to shape information environments, and how Meta profits from content and accounts tied to illegal settlement expansion and violent rhetoric against Palestinians.

items.title: Protest as a pillar of democracy

s: Protest helps close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we actually have
This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “ Protest in Democracy.
With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy.
You can support this coverage by donating here.

Democracy is often presented as an orderly, structured system of representation and deliberation, colorless and linear like an organizational version of the faux-classical architecture so many democratic countries adopt for their government buildings.
Voting leads to representatives, debates lead to votes on laws, participation leads to action, like columns leading to a pediment.
But democracy is not actually about cushy debating chambers or political speeches — or not only about that.

Democracy means rule by the people, and in most of the systems we call democracies today, the people’s role is for the most part narrowed to voting, and often a curtailed, difficult, limited vote that does little for accountability or expressing preferences on specific issues.
Protest is one of the ways we close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we have.

With protest, the people can express general emotional responses or very specific policy proposals; we can punctuate the long intervals of electoral cycles to influence government outside of the voting booth; and perhaps most importantly, we build coalitions and solidarity, forming a collective consciousness of our democratic responsibilities.
Voting is a single, standardized, and fairly isolated action.
Protest, on the other hand, unfolds in dozens, if not hundreds, of permutations, letting us — the people — express our creativity along with our civic engagement.

One of the wonderful things about this spotlight has been seeing the sheer range of capacity and ingenuity as people use protest to inspire others, express anger or determination, and pressure governments and other decision-makers.

Maybe the most obvious example of this in the spotlight is the collaborative article on protest music, with its examples of not just different songs, but different styles and approaches and even understanding of what it means to use music for advocacy.

In Japan, young people are finding new paths into activism, like handing out placards, while the Cockroach Janta Party in India has used memes and online jokes to mobilize young people right from the start of the movement.
Severe oppression requires more creativity, as this article about the evolution of street art in Russia points out.
Similarly, Russians — many of them in exile — used allusion and wordplay in online videos to get their messages across.
That raises the question, ably explored in this piece, about whether online and offline protest are equally effective, and what their different strengths and weaknesses are.
And, if the digital world has enabled new forms of protest, it has also activated new means of repression.
Our friends at Ranking Digital Rights contributed this well-researched article about the complicity of telecoms in internet shutdowns in Africa.
This piece, from AlgorithmWatch, details the Russian surveillance software being used against protesters in Georgia.
And the virtual world can be used to hijack, undermine, or redirect protest energy, as this case study from Funky Citizens in Romania details.
As vibrant as protests are in the moment, though, it’s also important to ask about the long-term impact, the consequences, both good and bad.

The protests in Bangladesh two years ago were successful in the sense that they led to a change of government; this article asks whether that change of government led to a meaningful difference in democratic accountability.
And this powerful piece from Nepal follows up with those involved in the Gen Z protests there last year, tracking the long-term impacts of injuries and trauma.

items.title: When Big Tech becomes a tool of state control in Kenya

s: State censorship on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them
This post by Grace Kobare is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism.
In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South.
You can support this coverage by donating here.

On January 30, 2018, Raila Odinga held his symbolic “swearing-in” ceremony in Nairobi, and the government, through Kenya’s regulator, switched off the transmitters of KTN, NTV and Citizen TV while they were broadcasting live.
The Interior Ministry defended the move, saying the media had been given a security briefing in advance.
The stations stayed off air for days and were only fully back by February 9, 2018.
The 2018 incident was just one of many examples of Kenyan officials cutting off connectivity — particularly during times of unrest.
During the June 2024 tax protests, authorities shut down internet connectivity for around seven hours and arrested a large number of protesters.
The Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) also reported that at least three networks blocked the web version of Telegram during those protests, and the blocks were reversed the same day.
A year later, during the June 2025 protests throughout Kenya, a communications authority issued a directive to media houses to stop live broadcasts of the unrest, and Telegram was blocked again.
Access Now said this violated a High Court injunction against interfering with internet and Telegram access.
Given these incidents, it is no surprise that Kenya’s internet freedom record has worsened in recent years.
Freedom House found that in 2025 Kenya had the most severe decline of the 72 countries assessed during the coverage period.
Kenya’s experience is part of a wider pattern.

Freedom House found that global internet freedom declined for the 15th consecutive year in 2025, as authoritarian governments used censorship and offline repression to crush protests organized online.

Access Now’s 2025 report found that at least 313 shutdowns were implemented globally, and that in Africa the internet was shut down 30 times in 15 countries, with protests the leading trigger, followed by elections.
In Tanzania, an internet blackout was imposed after protests erupted on election day, October 29, 2025.
It was only partially eased on November 4, alongside a curfew.
An opposition lawyer said online mobilization was part of the reason for the blanket block, and protesters used VPNs to reach platforms such as X Spaces.
In Uganda, the regulator ordered all mobile operators and internet providers to suspend public internet access nationwide from 6 p.m. on 13 January 2026, two days before the general election.
Officials had publicly denied plans for a blanket shutdown beforehand.

The platforms themselves have been targets too: A Facebook ban followed the five-day blackout of the 2021 election and was still in effect in 2026, and Starlink disabled its terminals in the country after Uganda ordered the service shut down on grounds they were unlicensed.
Kenya’s case shows how state pressure on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them.
The June 2025 Telegram block came despite a High Court injunction.
The government has also tried to write that power into law.
In October 2025, President William Ruto signed the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) said it risks criminalizing legitimate online speech.
The Act also expanded the powers of a state committee, the National Computer and Cybercrimes Coordination Committee (NC4), to make websites and apps inaccessible.
The High Court in Nairobi suspended key sections a week after Ruto signed it.
By July 2026, the High Court had declared the website-blocking powers unconstitutional.
The chairperson of the Bloggers Association of Kenya, Kennedy Kachwanya, told Human Rights Watch that the amended law poses an unacceptable threat to digital rights and freedom of expression.

items.title: Built for boats, adrift on land: Bangladesh’s Bede community struggles with a fixed-address system

s: Boats and people on the Turag River, Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Image via Flickr by Wonderlane. CC BY 2.0.
For nomadic Bede families on the Jamuna River in central Bangladesh, moving is a routine part of life.

A study published in May 2026 in the journal Cambridge Prisms: Global Mental Health looked at three nomadic settlements in Tangail district of central Bangladesh: Jugiyar Char, Palima and Char Nikrail.
It found that these families move several times a year, driven by seasonal floods and erosion, as well as searches for paying audiences.
However, climate change and increasingly unpredictable river conditions are forcing these communities to land.
The researchers conducted a micro-case study through 12 interviews and one focus group during Bangladesh’s 2025 monsoon season (June through October).
It describes displacement as an ongoing condition, not a single event.
“We cannot change the river, and we cannot stop moving,” one sardar, or community leader, told them.

A second study, published online in August 2026 in Dhaka University’s Social Science Review, highlights the dire environmental exposure and disaster vulnerabilities of Bede settlements in Munshiganj, calling for organized cooperation between government agencies and relief NGOs.
The Bede are a traditionally mobile community that has lived and worked on Bangladesh’s rivers for generations.
They have long been marginalized in Bangladeshi society, and many make a living as snake charmers, folk healers, sellers of herbal medicine and amulets, and street performers.
Historical accounts often trace the community’s roots to 1638, when groups arrived in Dhaka alongside the exiled king of Myanmar’s northwestern coastal region (then Arakan ).
It is difficult to get an accurate count of how many Bede exist in Bangladesh today.
Climate Watch, a Bangladeshi news site, has cited figures ranging from about 75,000, from the Department of Social Services, to roughly 800,000.
Families traditionally travel in boat groups led by a sardar (leader).
When they stop on land, they often camp on riverbanks or on chars, the sandbars that big rivers build up and wash away.
This is not ordinary migration.

Researchers from the study published in Cambridge Prisms: Global Mental Health contrast it with refugees who flee a single event: Bede families are almost always on the move, which makes them hard to reach for clinics, schools, and civil registers that assume a fixed address.
Today, many of these families are being forced to move away from their river roots and are settling on land.
Community members share that climate change has forced many to give up on the river as worsening floods, erosion, and storms make their former settlements uninhabitable.
They also said some canals and channels are drying up, making life on the water impossible in some areas.
In terms of income, one sardar explained that families stay about a month in one place and leave when audiences stop coming.

In Munshiganj, respondents told the Dhaka University team that demand for traditional work is falling, that stigma pushes people away from it, and that a recent ban on snake-catching has cost them income.
About 88 percent said they did not want their children to follow the traditional trades.

Concerning work on land, in 2019, leaders of the Bede settlement in Savar, near Dhaka, one of the country’s largest, told a police officer that poverty and dying rivers meant families could no longer sail to other areas, and that interest in snake-charming and other old trades was fading.
